deep.reconstruction: This is the title page and opening paragraph of E283, 'De numeris primis valde magnis' (Novi Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae 9, 1764). It contains no mathematics. It is a rhetorical preface. Euler says that nearly every geometer has wasted time looking for the order of the primes. He compares the 'law of progression' of the primes in arithmetic to the quadrature of the circle in geometry. Both seem hopeless, and both would, if found, have little direct use. Yet any method able to settle either problem would be of great value, because it would have overcome the main obstacles that have blocked these inquiries. Such a method would therefore promise great help throughout mathematics. The next page continues: such efforts should not be blamed even when they fail. It praises Fermat, recalls his challenge to Wallis to give a prime larger than any given number, and notes his conjecture that 2^(2^m)+1 is always prime. The later pages of the memoir deal with testing very large numbers for primality, notably through their representations as sums of two squares (e.g. numbers near 10^6). Its purpose is practical factorization and primality testing rather than a 'law' of the primes. The present page only motivates this.

ideas.what: Analogy: finding a law for the sequence of primes is as abstruse and apparently hopeless as squaring the circle; the method that solved either would matter more than the result itself
ideas.modern_name: Heuristic/methodological remark on the irregularity of prime distribution
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (a well-known quotable remark, cf. similar wording in his 1751 memoir on the sum of divisors)
ideas.where_published: E175 'Découverte d'une loi tout extraordinaire des nombres par rapport à la somme de leurs diviseurs' (written 1747, publ. 1751) opens with the similar claim that the order of the primes is a mystery the human mind may never penetrate; E283 itself

deep.surprise_reason: This is a purely rhetorical introduction with no mathematical content. The sentiment is a well-known and frequently quoted Euler remark, with close parallels in his other published works.
transcription_corrections: The page header '( o )' is a printer's ornament plus a decorative bracket, not text; otherwise the transcription matches the image closely (long-s forms and u/v spellings such as 'inueſtigando', 'vllus' are faithful to the print).
